questions.stem: In the somatic nervous system, which neurons carry information from sensory receptors to the central nervous system?
options: Autonomic motor neurons
Afferent (sensory) neurons
Efferent (motor) neurons
Interneurons within the brain
questions.explanation: Afferent neurons carry sensory information towards the central nervous system. Efferent neurons carry motor messages away from the central nervous system to muscles, so they travel in the opposite direction.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the autonomic nervous system?
options: Integrating sensory information in the cortex and initiating conscious decisions
Relaying touch and pain messages from the skin to the somatosensory cortex
Regulating visceral muscles, organs and glands, largely without conscious control
Carrying voluntary motor messages from the brain to the skeletal muscles
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system connects the central nervous system to the visceral muscles, organs and glands, and works largely unconsciously. Carrying voluntary messages to skeletal muscles is the role of the somatic nervous system.

questions.stem: Mia touches a hot saucepan and pulls her hand away before she feels any pain. Which sequence describes this spinal reflex?
options: Sensory neuron → interneuron in the spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle
Sensory neuron → brain → motor neuron in the spinal cord → muscle
Motor neuron → interneuron in the spinal cord → sensory neuron → muscle
Sensory neuron → interneuron in the brain stem → autonomic neuron → gland
questions.explanation: In a spinal reflex, the sensory neuron synapses with an interneuron in the spinal cord, which activates a motor neuron to the muscle. The brain is not needed to start the response, which is why it happens before Mia is aware of the pain.

questions.stem: Why does Mia feel pain only after her hand has already moved away from the saucepan?
options: Interneurons in the spinal cord block the pain message until the muscle has finished contracting
The sensory message also travels up the spinal cord to the brain, which takes longer than the reflex loop
Pain is processed by the autonomic nervous system, which transmits messages more slowly than the somatic system
The motor neuron must first signal the brain that the hand has moved before the pain message is sent
questions.explanation: While the reflex is initiated in the spinal cord, the sensory information also continues to the brain, where pain is perceived. That longer journey means awareness follows the movement. Pain from the skin is carried by the somatic nervous system, not the autonomic.

questions.stem: Which response is a conscious response carried out by the somatic nervous system?
options: Pupils dilating on walking into a dark cinema
Heart rate slowing while resting after lunch
Saliva flowing at the smell of cooking food
Reaching out to catch a ball a friend has thrown
questions.explanation: Catching a ball is a voluntary movement of skeletal muscles, planned by the brain and carried out by the somatic nervous system. Pupil size, heart rate and salivation are regulated unconsciously by the autonomic nervous system.

questions.stem: Once a threat has passed, which division of the nervous system returns the body to homeostasis?
options: Parasympathetic nervous system
Sympathetic nervous system
Somatic nervous system
Central nervous system
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic nervous system maintains and restores the body's optimal functioning, slowing heart rate and resuming digestion. The sympathetic nervous system is the division that arouses the body in response to a threat.

questions.stem: A person with a spinal cord injury in the neck still shows a knee-jerk reflex but cannot feel the tap on their knee. Which best explains this?
options: The reflex circuit in the lower spinal cord is intact, but sensory messages cannot travel up to the brain
The brain still initiates the reflex, but motor messages cannot travel down the spinal cord to the leg
The afferent neurons in the leg are damaged, but the efferent neurons in the leg are still intact
The autonomic nervous system has taken over the reflex because the somatic system is damaged
questions.explanation: A spinal reflex is organised in the spinal cord below the injury, so it still works. Feeling the tap requires sensory messages to ascend past the injury to the brain, which they cannot do. If the afferent neurons were damaged, the reflex itself could not occur.

questions.stem: Glutamate is best described as:
options: the main excitatory neurotransmitter, making a postsynaptic neuron more likely to fire
the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, making a postsynaptic neuron less likely to fire
a neuromodulator that acts slowly on many neurons at once to regulate mood
a hormone released into the blood by the adrenal glands during stress
questions.explanation: Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system. GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, which makes a postsynaptic neuron less likely to fire.

questions.stem: What is the effect of GABA on a postsynaptic neuron?
options: It acts as a neuromodulator that spreads across brain regions
It makes the neuron less likely to fire an action potential
It makes the neuron more likely to fire an action potential
It strengthens the synapse by triggering long-term potentiation
questions.explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, so it reduces the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will fire. Making the neuron more likely to fire is the excitatory effect of glutamate.

questions.stem: How does a neuromodulator such as dopamine differ from a neurotransmitter such as glutamate?
options: It acts at a single synapse and has a rapid, brief effect on one postsynaptic neuron only
It is released into the bloodstream by endocrine glands rather than by neurons
It always inhibits postsynaptic neurons, whereas neurotransmitters always excite them
It is released over a wider area and affects many neurons, with slower, longer-lasting effects
questions.explanation: Neuromodulators are released by neurons but diffuse more widely, influencing the activity of many neurons over a longer time. Fast, brief action at one synapse describes a neurotransmitter such as glutamate. Neuromodulators come from neurons, not endocrine glands.

questions.stem: Which statement about serotonin is correct?
options: It is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that acts only within the spinal cord
It is a neuromodulator involved in regulating mood, sleep and appetite
It is the main excitatory neurotransmitter involved in learning new skills
It is the hormone released by the adrenal glands during chronic stress
questions.explanation: Serotonin is a neuromodulator with widespread effects, including on mood, sleep and appetite. The main excitatory neurotransmitter is glutamate, and the hormone released in chronic stress is cortisol.

questions.stem: A drug blocks glutamate receptor sites on postsynaptic neurons in the hippocampus. What is the most likely effect?
options: Increased excitation of the postsynaptic neurons, strengthening long-term potentiation
Increased GABA release, so the presynaptic neurons stop releasing neurotransmitter
Reduced dopamine release, so neuromodulation of the reward pathways stops entirely
Reduced excitation of the postsynaptic neurons, impairing long-term potentiation
questions.explanation: If glutamate cannot bind to its receptors, the postsynaptic neurons receive less excitation. Long-term potentiation depends on repeated glutamate activity, so it would be impaired. Blocking receptors cannot increase excitation, because the excitatory signal is the one being blocked.

questions.stem: Long-term potentiation refers to:
options: the growth of new neurons in the hippocampus throughout adulthood
the long-lasting strengthening of synaptic connections after repeated stimulation
the long-lasting weakening of synaptic connections that receive low or no stimulation
the removal of unused synaptic connections during brain development
questions.explanation: Long-term potentiation is the long-lasting strengthening of synaptic connections that results from repeated activation. The long-lasting weakening of connections through lack of stimulation is long-term depression.

questions.stem: Elena practises a dance routine every day and it becomes easier to perform. A piano piece she has not played for years has become hard to recall. Which processes best explain each change?
options: Sprouting for the dance; long-term potentiation for the piano piece
Pruning for the dance; sprouting for the piano piece
Long-term potentiation for the dance; long-term depression for the piano piece
Long-term depression for the dance; long-term potentiation for the piano piece
questions.explanation: Repeated practice strengthens the synapses involved through long-term potentiation. Synapses that go unused for a long time weaken through long-term depression, making the piano piece harder to retrieve. Long-term potentiation strengthens connections, so it cannot explain a skill fading.

questions.stem: An undamaged neuron loses its connection with another neuron and forms a new connection with a different active neuron. This is called:
options: long-term depression
rerouting
sprouting
pruning
questions.explanation: Rerouting is when a neuron that has lost a connection forms a new one with another active neuron, creating an alternative pathway. Sprouting is the growth of new extensions, such as dendrites and axon branches, on a neuron.

questions.stem: Synaptic pruning is:
options: the formation of a new neural pathway around damaged tissue
the elimination of synaptic connections that are rarely used
the growth of new dendrites and axon terminals on a neuron
the strengthening of synaptic connections that are used often
questions.explanation: Pruning removes weak or unused synaptic connections, making neural networks more efficient. The growth of new dendrites and axon terminals is sprouting, which adds connections rather than removing them.

questions.stem: Why is synaptic plasticity described as the fundamental mechanism of memory formation that leads to learning?
options: LTP and LTD change the strength of synaptic connections, so experience physically modifies neural pathways
Each new memory causes a new neuron to grow in the cortex, so learning is simply the steady addition of new brain cells
Neuromodulators carry each memory between the hippocampus and cerebellum, where it is copied during sleep
Each memory is stored at a single synapse, which GABA strengthens every time the memory is retrieved
questions.explanation: Learning and memory are encoded as changes to synaptic connections: long-term potentiation strengthens them and long-term depression weakens them, along with sprouting, rerouting and pruning. Memories are distributed across networks of neurons rather than added as new cells or stored at one synapse.

questions.stem: Which is an internal stressor?
options: A noisy construction site next to the house
An argument with a sibling over chores
A deadline for a major school assignment next week
Persistent worry about not being good enough
questions.explanation: Internal stressors come from within the person, such as their own thoughts, worries or illness. Noise, arguments and deadlines are external stressors, because they come from the environment.

questions.stem: Which is a psychological response to stress rather than a physiological one?
options: Increased sweating
Difficulty concentrating
Increased heart and breathing rates
Tense shoulder muscles
questions.explanation: Psychological stress responses affect thoughts, feelings and behaviour, such as difficulty concentrating, irritability or worry. Heart rate, muscle tension and sweating are physiological changes in the body.

questions.stem: During the flight-or-fight response, which pair of changes occurs?
options: Heart rate slows and breathing deepens
Saliva increases and the bladder contracts
Pupils dilate and digestion slows
Pupils constrict and digestion speeds up
questions.explanation: Activation of the sympathetic nervous system dilates the pupils and slows non-essential functions such as digestion, freeing energy to deal with the threat. Constricted pupils and increased digestion are parasympathetic effects.

questions.stem: Ari freezes when a large snake appears on the walking track a metre ahead of him. Why can the freeze response be adaptive in a situation like this?
options: Freezing is a conscious decision made through his somatic nervous system to save energy
Freezing moves his body directly into the exhaustion stage, so it can rest and recover
Staying still may stop the threat noticing him when fighting or fleeing is unlikely to succeed
Freezing gives his parasympathetic nervous system time to stop all cortisol release at once
questions.explanation: The freeze response is an involuntary reaction that can help a person avoid detection or further harm when fight or flight is unlikely to succeed. It is not a conscious decision, and it is part of the acute stress response, not the exhaustion stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome.

questions.stem: In chronic stress, prolonged high levels of cortisol are most likely to:
options: activate the parasympathetic nervous system to calm the body down
reduce the amount of glucose available to the body for energy
suppress the immune system, increasing vulnerability to illness
strengthen the immune system, protecting the body from infection
questions.explanation: Cortisol helps the body sustain its response to a stressor, but over long periods it suppresses immune functioning, so a person becomes more susceptible to illness. Cortisol raises, rather than lowers, the glucose available for energy.

questions.stem: How does the role of cortisol in the stress response differ from that of adrenaline?
options: Cortisol produces the immediate burst of arousal in acute stress; adrenaline maintains arousal for weeks
Cortisol is released by neurons as a neurotransmitter; adrenaline is released by the gut microbiota
Cortisol activates the parasympathetic nervous system; adrenaline activates the somatic nervous system
Cortisol maintains energy over a longer period; adrenaline produces a rapid, short-lived burst of arousal
questions.explanation: Adrenaline is released quickly under sympathetic activation and produces the immediate physiological arousal of the flight-or-fight response. Cortisol is released more slowly and keeps energy available over a longer period, which is why it is linked with chronic stress.

questions.stem: The gut–brain axis refers to:
options: the two-way communication network linking the gut and the central nervous system
a one-way pathway through which the brain alone controls the speed of digestion in the gut
the spinal reflex that triggers vomiting when unsafe food is swallowed
the region of the brain stem that produces feelings of hunger and fullness
questions.explanation: The gut–brain axis is bidirectional: the brain influences the gut, and the gut, including its microbiota, influences the brain. Describing it as one-way, from brain to gut, misses the influence of the gut on psychological processes.

questions.stem: Which nerve is a major pathway for communication between the gut and the brain?
options: Optic nerve
Sciatic nerve
Auditory nerve
Vagus nerve
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve connects the brain stem with many internal organs, including the gut, and carries messages in both directions. The optic and auditory nerves carry visual and sound information, and the sciatic nerve serves the legs.

questions.stem: Which finding best illustrates the interaction of gut microbiota with stress?
options: Gut microbiota release cortisol directly into the blood, replacing the adrenal glands in chronic stress
Stress influences the gut only through the somatic nervous system and never through the vagus nerve
Gut microbiota influence digestion, but no pathway exists for them to influence the brain
Psychological stress can alter the composition of gut microbiota, which can in turn affect mood and behaviour
questions.explanation: Research suggests stress can change the balance of gut microbiota, and changes in the microbiota can influence the brain, mood and behaviour. Cortisol is released by the adrenal glands, not by gut microbiota, and the vagus nerve is a key pathway for this communication.

questions.stem: Mice raised with no gut microbiota showed an exaggerated stress hormone response, which was reduced when certain gut bacteria were introduced. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: Adding these bacteria to the human gut will cure chronic stress in most people
The stress response in mice is controlled by the gut microbiota alone, without involving the brain
Gut microbiota can influence the stress response, but findings in mice may not apply to humans
Gut microbiota are the only cause of the stress response, in both mice and humans
questions.explanation: The results show that gut microbiota can influence the stress response in mice, but animal findings need testing in humans before they can be generalised. The study does not show that microbiota are the only cause, or that the brain plays no part.

questions.stem: Why is the gut–brain axis described as an area of emerging research?
options: Much of the evidence comes from animal studies, and causal links in humans are still being established
It has been fully explained, and its findings are now used to diagnose every mental disorder
It was abandoned after early animal studies failed to find any link between the gut and the brain at all
It can only be studied through post-mortem examination of human brain tissue
questions.explanation: Research into the gut–brain axis is growing, but much of it uses animals or correlational designs, so how gut microbiota cause changes in human psychological processes is not yet settled. That is what makes it emerging rather than established.

questions.stem: What are the three stages of Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome, in order?
options: Shock, countershock, alarm reaction
Alarm reaction, resistance, exhaustion
Resistance, alarm reaction, exhaustion
Alarm reaction, exhaustion, resistance
questions.explanation: The General Adaptation Syndrome begins with the alarm reaction, then resistance, then exhaustion if the stressor continues. Shock and countershock are the two phases within the alarm reaction stage, not separate stages.

questions.stem: During the shock phase of the alarm reaction stage, the body's resistance to stress:
options: drops below its normal level
rises well above its normal level
remains at its normal level
rises steadily until exhaustion
questions.explanation: In shock, the body reacts as if injured and its resistance briefly falls below normal, for example blood pressure and body temperature may drop. Resistance rises above normal in countershock, when the sympathetic nervous system is activated.

questions.stem: Which stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome involves sustained high cortisol levels and resistance above normal as the body focuses its resources on the stressor?
options: Countershock
Shock
Exhaustion
Resistance
questions.explanation: In the resistance stage, cortisol keeps energy available and resistance to the stressor stays above normal. Countershock also raises resistance, but it is the brief sympathetic arousal at the start, driven mainly by adrenaline.

questions.stem: After months of ongoing financial stress, Sam's resources are depleted and he keeps getting sick. According to the General Adaptation Syndrome, which stage is Sam in?
options: Resistance
Countershock
Shock
Exhaustion
questions.explanation: In exhaustion, the body's resources are depleted and resistance drops below normal, so illness becomes more likely. During resistance the body is still coping, with resistance above normal.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of the General Adaptation Syndrome as a model of stress?
options: It cannot explain why prolonged exposure to a stressor is associated with an increased risk of illness
It describes psychological responses only and ignores physiological ones
It was developed mainly from interviews with human participants
It does not account for how a person's appraisal of a stressor can change their response
questions.explanation: The General Adaptation Syndrome describes a general physiological pattern and does not consider cognitive factors such as appraisal, so it cannot explain why people respond differently to the same stressor. It does explain illness in exhaustion, and it was based mainly on research with rats.

questions.stem: Two students sit the same exam. One shows a strong stress response, while the other feels excited and calm. Why does this observation support Lazarus and Folkman's model more than Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome?
options: The GAS applies only to physical stressors, whereas the Transactional Model applies only to exams
The Transactional Model explains individual differences through appraisal; the GAS predicts one pattern for any stressor
The GAS explains individual differences through secondary appraisal, whereas the Transactional Model ignores such differences
The Transactional Model describes three physiological stages of stress, which the GAS does not include
questions.explanation: Lazarus and Folkman explain stress as depending on how each person appraises a situation, so different reactions to the same exam are expected. The GAS proposes a similar physiological pattern for any stressor. Secondary appraisal belongs to the Transactional Model, not the GAS.

questions.stem: During countershock, what happens to the body?
options: The parasympathetic nervous system dominates and resistance falls below normal
The body's resources are used up and resistance falls to its lowest level
Cortisol stops being released and the body returns to its normal level
The sympathetic nervous system is activated and resistance rises above normal
questions.explanation: In countershock the sympathetic nervous system is activated, releasing adrenaline, and resistance rises above normal. Resistance falls below normal in shock, and resources are depleted in exhaustion.

questions.stem: In Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model of Stress and Coping, primary appraisal involves evaluating:
options: whether one has the resources to cope with a stressful situation
which stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome the body has reached
how well a coping strategy worked after the stressor has ended
whether a situation is irrelevant, benign-positive or stressful
questions.explanation: In primary appraisal a person judges the significance of the situation: irrelevant, benign-positive or stressful, and if stressful, whether it is harm/loss, threat or challenge. Evaluating coping resources is secondary appraisal.

questions.stem: In the Transactional Model, secondary appraisal involves:
options: evaluating the coping resources and options available to deal with the stressor
deciding whether the stressful situation is a harm/loss, a threat or a challenge to the person
measuring the physiological changes that follow exposure to a stressor
re-experiencing the stressor in memory after it has ended
questions.explanation: Secondary appraisal is the evaluation of internal and external resources for coping. Judging a stressful situation as harm/loss, threat or challenge happens in primary appraisal.

questions.stem: Jo feels nervous about a job interview but thinks, 'This is a chance to show what I can do.' In primary appraisal, Jo has judged the situation to be a:
options: benign-positive situation
challenge
threat
harm/loss
questions.explanation: Jo sees the interview as stressful but with potential for gain or growth, which is a challenge appraisal. A threat appraisal focuses on harm that might happen, and a benign-positive situation is not appraised as stressful at all.

questions.stem: Tara appraises an upcoming debate as a threat. She then realises her teacher will help her prepare and that she has argued similar topics before. According to the Transactional Model, what is most likely to happen?
options: Her primary appraisal changes the debate into an irrelevant situation
She moves from the resistance stage into the exhaustion stage
Her stress increases, because secondary appraisal always adds to a threat
Her secondary appraisal that she has adequate resources reduces her stress
questions.explanation: When secondary appraisal shows that coping resources are adequate, the person experiences less stress. Tara still sees the debate as relevant; what changed is her judgement of her resources. Resistance and exhaustion are stages of Selye's model, not this one.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping?
options: It explains stress through physiological stages and ignores thoughts
Appraisals are subjective and can change quickly, so they are difficult to measure
It cannot account for differences between people in response to the same stressor
It is based on experiments with rats, so it may not apply to humans
questions.explanation: Because appraisal is a personal mental process that can shift as a situation unfolds, it is hard to measure objectively and test. Explaining individual differences is a strength of the model, and research with rats was the basis of Selye's model.

questions.stem: An approach coping strategy is one that:
options: denies that the stressor exists or that it is important
confronts the stressor directly to reduce or resolve it
evades the stressor so that it does not have to be faced
delays dealing with the stressor in the hope it goes away
questions.explanation: Approach strategies deal directly with the stressor or its effects, such as making a plan or seeking information. Evading, delaying and denying are all avoidance strategies.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an avoidance coping strategy?
options: Making a study timetable for the weeks leading up to an exam
Asking a teacher to explain an exam topic that is confusing
Working through past exam papers to find weak areas
Scrolling on a phone for hours to avoid thinking about an exam
questions.explanation: Avoidance strategies evade the stressor rather than dealing with it, as scrolling to stop thinking about an exam does. Planning, asking for help and practising all confront the stressor directly, so they are approach strategies.

questions.stem: Coping flexibility is best described as:
options: the use of the same coping strategy for every kind of stressor to build consistency over time
the use of avoidance strategies whenever approach strategies feel too demanding
the match between the coping strategy chosen and the features of the stressor
the ability to recognise when a strategy is not working and switch to a more suitable one
questions.explanation: Coping flexibility is the ability to notice that a strategy is ineffective and to change to another one. The match between a strategy and the stressor is context-specific effectiveness, a related but separate idea.

questions.stem: Leo uses problem-solving to settle a disagreement with a friend, and it works. When his grandmother becomes seriously ill, problem-solving does little to help, so he starts talking with his family about his feelings. Leo's change of strategy best demonstrates:
options: avoidance coping
primary appraisal
coping flexibility
the resistance stage
questions.explanation: Leo recognised that his usual strategy did not suit the new stressor and switched to a different one, which is coping flexibility. Talking with family confronts his feelings about the illness, so it is not avoidance.

questions.stem: Wen is waiting two days for medical test results that she cannot influence. She watches a favourite film to take her mind off them. This is best described as:
options: secondary appraisal, because she is evaluating whether she can cope
an avoidance strategy that may be effective in the short term in this context
an approach strategy, because it reduces her stress directly at its source
an avoidance strategy that will always be ineffective and harmful for her
questions.explanation: Distraction avoids the stressor, so it is an avoidance strategy. Because Wen cannot change the result, distraction may suit this context and reduce distress in the short term, which shows that effectiveness depends on the context. Avoidance is not always harmful.
